title: Autonomic networking
summary:
Autonomic networking follows the concept of Autonomic Computing, an initiative started by IBM in 2001. Its ultimate aim is to create self-managing networks to overcome the rapidly growing complexity of the Internet and other networks and to enable their further growth, far beyond the size of today.

The fundamental goal is self-management, including self-configuration, self-optimization, self-healing, and self-protection. This is achieved by an autonomic function having minimal dependencies on human administrators or centralized management systems, and it usually implies distribution across network elements. Instead of a layering approach, autonomic networking targets a more flexible structure termed compartmentalization, with the goal of producing an architectural design that enables flexible, dynamic, and fully autonomic formation of large-scale networks.

Key sub-systems of autonomic networking include: Autognostics (monitoring), which provides the system with self-knowledge through discovery, awareness, and analysis capabilities; Configuration Management, responsible for interaction with network elements and interfaces with historical tracking; Policy Management, requiring a flexible and abstract framework of values, relationships, roles, and interactions; Autodefense, a dynamic and adaptive mechanism that responds to malicious attacks on the network infrastructure; and Connection Fabric, which supports interaction with all elements and sub-systems.

The primary goal of autonomic systems is not to remove humans from the process, but rather to shift the burden of maintenance and management from people to technology to alleviate tedious, repetitive tasks. The IETF has been actively working on standardization through RFC 7575 and the ANIMA (Autonomic Networking Integrated Model and Approach) working group.
